paper_title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Live game streaming has become one of the largest forms of online video, and commentary is what turns raw gameplay into show. good caster reacts the moment something happens and tells the audience who just appeared, what item was picked up and where the fight is taking place. Automating this requires video model that watches an unbounded stream, decides every second whether to speak, and says something both timely and correct about the game world. Video LLMs [3, 19, 21, 40] understand short clips well, and streaming video LLMs [6, 7, 30, 42, 43, 46, 52] decide frame by frame whether to respond. Automatic commentary was first studied for sports and esports [26, 31, 37, 51], where the teams and rules are known in advance. Proact-VL [47] recently brought streaming video LLMs to game commentary and reports strong timing and quality on multi-game benchmark. These systems are trained and evaluated on the same games. In practice commentator constantly meets titles, characters and items it has never seen, and the entities that make commentary informative are exactly the ones that change from one game to the next. We therefore study cross-game streaming commentary, in which model is trained on single game and commentates games that never appear in training. Under this setting the standard recipe breaks down in revealing way  (Fig. 1)  . Retrained on Baldurs Gate 3 alone, Proact-VL commentator rarely names what is on screen in ten unseen games, and when it does, it often reaches for its training game, for example calling character in Tears of the Kingdom Karlach. Timing transfers across games, but knowledge does not. natural remedy is to give the model the missing knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation [2, 15, 18, 24], tool-using agents [16, 34, 50] and multi-agent systems [44] all supply external information to model. Live commentary, however, imposes constraints these methods do not address. Knowledge retrieved before the stream starts is mostly irrelevant to the current second, and in our experiments game-level dossier barely changes what the commentator says. Retrieving at every second floods the context. Text queries are further bottleneck, since the commentator would have to describe in words something it cannot recognize. Most importantly, the commentator must decide when an answer is worth asking for, which depends on what this particular model does not know. Language models can partly tell what they do not know [13, 17, 41], but streaming video models have no such mechanism. We propose StreamDuo, two-agent streaming commentator. commentator agent watches the stream and talks. When it sees something it cannot name, it asks research agent by sending the current frames. The research agent, frozen vision-language model with access to the games wiki, returns few entries two seconds later while the stream continues. Perception and language, which transfer across games, stay in the commentator, and game-specific knowledge is looked up at test time in whatever game is being played. We train only the commentator, and only on the source game, in two stages. The first teaches it when to ask, with ask labels placed where an answer would actually help the model reproduce what the human caster said. The second teaches it how to use noisy answers, through on-policy self-distillation [54] from privileged copy of itself that sees an ideal answer containing the right entry. On ten unseen games, StreamDuo reduces source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0% and raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 compared with Proact-VL trained on the same data, while also improving timing and the commentary quality judged by an LLM on all ten test games. In summary, our contributions are as follows. We formulate cross-game streaming commentary, together with clean evaluation protocol and source-game leakage metric, and show that current streaming commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, two-agent commentator that asks frozen research agent with frames and receives its answers while the stream continues, trained with information-gain ask labels and on-policy self-distillation from privileged copy of itself. On ten unseen games, StreamDuo outperforms zero-shot streaming models, Proact-VL retrained on the same data, and the same models given the research agents knowledge without interaction.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Streaming video LLMs and live commentary. Video LLMs understand complete clips [3, 1921, 40, 45], and streaming variants process frames as they arrive, either by managing memory over long streams [8, 10, 29, 36, 46, 52] or by deciding when to respond without being prompted [6, 30, 39, 42, 43, 49], as measured by online benchmarks [22, 27]. LiveCC [7] and Proact-VL [47] bring this to live commentary. Earlier commentary systems targeted single domain such as chess [14], soccer [26, 28, 31], racing [12] or esports [37, 51, 53], often with structured game data. All of these models speak from what is in their weights and context, and are evaluated on the domains they are trained on. We test on games whose entities are never seen in training and let the commentator obtain the missing knowledge while the stream runs. Retrieval, tools and multiple agents. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies external text [18], and adaptive variants retrieve only when the model is uncertain [2, 13, 15, 17, 41]. Knowledge-based visual question answering retrieves encyclopedic entries for an image [5, 25, 48], and video RAG retrieves auxiliary text for video understanding [24]. Tool-using agents call search while reasoning [16, 34, 50], and multi-agent frameworks let models with different roles cooperate [44]. In StreamDuo the query is the frames themselves, the answer arrives after delay while the commentator keeps talking, and the decision to ask is learned from how much an answer would change this particular models output. Distillation with privileged information. teacher with access to information unavailable at test time can guide student [23, 38], and on-policy distillation trains the student on its own samples [1, 9] to avoid the mismatch between training on reference sequences and generating at test time [4, 33]. On-policy self-distillation [54] uses the same model, conditioned on privileged information, as its own teacher. We apply it to two-agent setting in which the privileged information is the answer the research agent should have returned, and sharpen the teachers use of that answer with context-aware decoding [35].

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Our goal is commentator that keeps talking at the right moments in game it has never seen, and that says the right names when it does. We first describe the streaming setting and why it fails across games (Sec. 3.1). We then present StreamDuo, which pairs the commentator with research agent (Sec. 3.2), and the two training stages that teach the commentator when to ask (Sec. 3.3) and how to use what it is told (Sec. 3.4). Fig. 2 illustrates the whole pipeline.

sections.title: 3.1 Streaming commentary across games
sections.content: A live stream arrives one second at time. At second the commentator receives the frames vt of that second and short history ht made of the co-commentators last line and its own recent lines. Following Proact-VL [47], each second is one turn of video LLM πθ. The turn ends with special flag token whose hidden state zt feeds response head, which outputs the probability pt = σ(w zt) that the commentator If it speaks, the language model generates short line yt πθ( ht, vt), and should speak now. otherwise it stays silent. Both parts are trained on human commentary with language-modeling loss on the spoken lines and binary loss on the speak decisions, Lbase = LLM + Lspk. (1) In cross-game commentary, πθ is trained on single source game Gs and evaluated on unseen games Gt = Gs. The two parts of the model behave very differently under this shift. When to speak depends on what happens on screen, such as fight starting or menu opening, and transfers well. What to say about the entities on screen depends on knowledge of the game world, and model trained on one game only knows that one. Faced with an unfamiliar character, it either describes it vaguely or reaches for name it learned from the source game. To keep the model from tying names to what it memorized, we rename the entities of the source game consistently and at random during training, so that name in the training data is evidence only within its own clip. This removes the shortcut but cannot supply the names of new game. That knowledge has to come from somewhere else at test time. 3 Figure 2 Overview of StreamDuo. Top: on an unseen game, the commentator asks the frozen research agent with the current frames, and the wiki entry it returns two seconds later lets the commentator name what is on screen. Bottom left: Stage 1 labels an ask only where an answer would make the human line more likely. Bottom right: Stage 2 distills frozen copy of the commentator that sees the ideal answer into the student that sees the noisy one.

sections.title: 3.2 StreamDuo
sections.content: StreamDuo splits the job between two agents with complementary strengths. The commentator agent πθ watches every second of the stream and decides when to talk, but only knows the game it was trained on. The research agent sees nothing of the stream unless asked, but can read the wiki of whatever game is being played. Commentary emerges from their exchange. The commentator notices that it does not recognize something, the research agent identifies it, and the commentator turns the answer into line. The commentator asks with frames. natural interface would be text query, but model that cannot recognize character also cannot describe it well enough to retrieve it. The commentator therefore sends the frames themselves. second head on the same flag state estimates whether an answer is needed, qt = σ(w zt), (2) and the commentator sends vt to the research agent when qt exceeds threshold. The research agent looks and searches. The research agent is frozen vision-language model with search tool over the games wiki. Before the stream starts, it writes short dossier of the game, which the commentator receives as general background. The dossier cannot say which of its entities is on screen at given second, so the real work happens when question arrives. The research agent looks at the frames it was sent, proposes few search keys from what it sees, including any names readable on screen, searches the wiki, looks at the frames again to check the candidates, and returns up to three entries, each with name, type and one-line description. We write the returned answer as At. Because the research agent reads the frames rather than description of them, it can identify character the commentator could never have described in text query. 4 Answers arrive while the stream continues. Looking things up takes time, and the stream does not wait. The answer to question asked at second arrives δ seconds later and is placed in the history ht+δ, where it stays available for the following seconds. Meanwhile the commentator keeps deciding every second whether to speak. This asynchrony is part of the problem the commentator has to learn to live with. It must ask before it needs the answer, and connect an answer to what it is seeing when the answer arrives. Speaking and stopping. An answer often gives the commentator something to say, and model that has started an explanation tends to keep going after the moment passes. We therefore use higher bar for continuing than for starting. The commentator starts speaking when pt exceeds τ, and after run of spoken seconds continues only when pt exceeds larger threshold τc. It can thus react immediately to new events and stop once the event ends. Only the commentator is trained, and only on the source game. The research agent stays frozen and brings its knowledge from the wiki of the game at hand, so the same pair can be pointed at any game for which wiki exists. The commentator has to learn two things that standard training does not teach, namely when an answer is worth asking for and how to turn noisy answer into the right line.

sections.title: 3.3 Learning when to ask
sections.content: The obvious supervision for the ask head is to ask shortly before the human caster names an entity. This ignores the one thing that makes asking useful, which is whether the model already knows the answer. model that reliably recognizes the protagonist gains nothing from asking about her, while model that cannot tell two bosses apart gains lot. The label should depend on the model. We define the value of asking through the model itself. Let ya be the line the human says at second and let be an ideal answer that contains the entity named in ya. frozen copy of the commentator, πθ0, scores this line twice, once with the answer in its history and once without it. The information gain ga = log πθ0 (ya ha, , va) log πθ0 (ya ha, va) (3) measures how much the answer helps the model say what the caster said. We label second δ as an ask moment when ga > γ, so that the answer would arrive in time. Lines the model can already produce receive no label because their gain is small, and so do lines that no answer could help with, such as tactical remarks. What remains are the moments when the model does not know and an answer would fix it. The ask head is trained with binary loss on these labels together with the base objective, L1 = LLM + Lspk + λ Lask. (4) In the same stage the commentator learns to read answers. During training, each answer placed in the history contains the entity the caster names next together with distractor entries from the same game, and some answers miss the entity altogether, mimicking what real research agent returns. Because entity names are randomly renamed in each clip, the model cannot have memorized them and must take them from the answer that it receives.

sections.title: 3.4 Learning to use the answer
sections.content: Supervised training on answers teaches the format of an answer but not how to use it. The answers the commentator receives at test time come from real research agent. They are often plausible but wrong, and the right entry, when present, is mixed with others. model fine-tuned to copy entries from its history will repeat whatever arrives, and model that ignores its history will never say the new names. What we want is model that uses an entry when it matches the frames and otherwise does not. We obtain this behavior with on-policy self-distillation [54]. The student is the commentator πθ, which sees noisy answer exactly as it would at test time. The teacher is frozen copy of the same model, πθ0, which sees the ideal answer for the same moment. The teacher is not larger model. It knows more only because it is told which entry is right, and its behavior shows what using that entry looks like. 5 The effect of an answer on fine-tuned model is often small, because the model has learned to rely on the frames and its own memory. We make the teachers use of the answer explicit by contrasting its predictions with and without the answer [35], log pT() = log softmax (cid:16) (1 + α) ℓθ0 ( A) α ℓθ0 ( ) (cid:17) , (5) where ℓθ0 denotes the teachers next-token logits given the same frames and history and α 0 controls the amplification. Tokens that become likely because of the answer, such as the name of the entity on screen, are pushed up, and tokens the model would say anyway are left unchanged. Training is on-policy. For moment right after an answer arrives, the student samples its own lines ˆy πθ( h, A, v), and the teacher scores each of their tokens. We minimize the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence over the students samples, L2 = ˆyπθ (cid:104) KL(cid:0)πθ( ˆy<k, h, A, v) (cid:13) (cid:13) pT( ˆy<k)(cid:1)(cid:105) . (6) Sampling from the student matters here. The student is corrected on the lines it would actually say, including the ones where it repeats wrong entry, rather than on human lines it would never produce. The reverse divergence makes the student commit to what the teacher considers likely instead of spreading its probability over every name in the answer. Only small set of low-rank adapter weights is updated in this stage, so the speaking behavior learned before is preserved, and the teacher is simply the model with the LoRA adapter switched off during its forward pass. At test time neither the teacher nor the ideal answer is used. The commentator watches the stream, asks with its frames when its ask head fires, and speaks with whatever the research agent returns.

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Data. We use the game commentary benchmark of Proact-VL [47], training on 10,286 Baldurs Gate 3 clips and testing on 2,470 clips from ten other games, from open-world adventures such as Tears of the Kingdom to esports such as League of Legends. The original inputs leak game knowledge through the caster persona, the earlier transcript and the other casters lines. We therefore keep only the personas speaking style, remove earlier transcripts and replace game-specific names in the other casters lines with typed placeholders such as [PLAYER]. Game knowledge can then only come from the wiki of 190,722 pages. Metrics. For timing we report TimeDiff and F1 of Proact-VL. For knowledge we match wiki entities in the two commentaries. Ent-R is the share of the humans entities that the model also names, Ent-F1 adds precision, and K-strict counts only lines that need game knowledge. These count the first 126 words of each clip, twice the human average, so that talking more cannot raise recall. Qwen3-30B [3] scores PAUC, CC, LiveU and FinalQ of Proact-VL on all test clips. Baselines. We compare with streaming video LLMs that decide when to respond, VideoLLM-online [6], LiveCC [7], Dispider [30], MMDuet [42], StreamingVLM [46], MMDuet2 [43] and Proact-VL [47], each with its official code and the game title as context. We test them zero-shot and after one epoch on the same Baldurs Gate 3 clips with the official recipe. Proact-VL has seen the test games, so we retrain it from LiveCC-7B-Base. Dispider releases no training code, and for MMDuet2 we rerun only the supervised stage. Each trained baseline is also given the research agents dossier, to separate the knowledge itself from the way in which StreamDuo obtains it during the stream. Implementation. The commentator starts from LiveCC-7B-Base [7], as Proact-VL does. Stage 1 fine-tunes all parameters for one epoch at learning rate of 105 with γ = 1 nat. Stage 2 trains rank-32 LoRA [11] for 300 steps with α = 1. The research agent is Qwen3-VL-8B [3] with BM25 search [32] and returns up to three entries after δ = 2 s. At test time it speaks when pt > 0.27 and asks when qt > 0.9. All runs use eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs for training and evaluation. 6 Table 1 Cross-game streaming commentary. Models are trained on Baldurs Gate 3 only (or not trained) and evaluated on 2,470 clips from ten unseen games. Knowledge metrics use the first 126 words of each clip (twice the human average), so model cannot gain recall by talking more. Judge metrics are scored by Qwen3-30B. Supervised stage of the official recipe only, without RL. Bold: best; underline: second best. sections.title: 4.2 Main results
sections.content: Tab. 1 shows that existing streaming models fail on unseen games in two ways. Zero-shot, they rarely speak at the right moments. LiveCC names the most entities among them but has TimeDiff of 3.03 s, and the others either stay silent or describe the scene. After training on Baldurs Gate 3, Proact-VL and StreamingVLM learn when to speak, but their entity recall stays below that of zero-shot LiveCC, and VideoLLM-online speaks more often without naming single correct entity. Models that decide silence through their language output, such as LiveCC and MMDuet2, collapse to few words per clip and mostly read the dialogue shown on screen. Timing transfers across games, knowledge does not. Adding the research agents game dossier to their context barely helps, for example raising the K-strict of Proact-VL by only 0.003, since dossier covers the whole game but cannot tell which entity is on screen. StreamDuo is best on all metrics except CC. Compared with Proact-VL, trained from the same base on the same clips, it raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 and K-strict from 0.085 to 0.127, while responding faster and receiving higher judge scores. It also names more entities than zero-shot LiveCC without giving up timing. CC favors near-silent models in this comparison, such as MMDuet2 with few words per clip, and does not reflect the quality of the commentary itself.

sections.title: 4.3 Contribution of each component
sections.content: Tab. 2 adds the components of StreamDuo one at time, all with the same inference settings. The first row follows the recipe of Proact-VL. Renaming the entities of the source game and adding the dossier do not raise entity recall (0.082 to 0.083), which agrees with the dossier results in Tab. 1, but they make the commentary more natural, raising LiveU from 4.91 to 5.03. Asking the research agent with the frames adds what the dossier cannot provide, the identity of what is on screen, and lifts Ent-R to 0.092 while also improving timing. sections.title: 4.5 When does the commentator ask?
sections.content: Fig. 3 aligns the commentary of StreamDuo with its own questions on the test games. Questions are rare, 264 over 2,470 clips. Before question, the commentator names an entity in only 1 to 4% of the seconds, below the 7% of random second, so it asks when it has no name to offer. When the answer arrives two seconds later, the share jumps to 32%, 4.6 times that of random second. It stays above the random rate for five more seconds, at 22% one and two seconds after the answer and 12% five seconds after it, and returns to the base rate within about eight seconds. The jump comes from the answer and not from the scene. With asking disabled, the same seconds name an entity only 5% of the time. The commentator thus uses an answer at once. Figure 3 Entity naming around questions (orange) and random seconds (blue). The answer arrives at 2 s.

sections.title: 4.6 What Stage 2 needs
sections.content: Fig. 4 varies the loss and the teacher of Stage 2. Fine-tuning on the real answers of the research agent gives the lowest TimeDiff and higher LiveU, but entity recall falls below that of Stage 1 (0.086 against 0.092). Without amplification (α = 0) the gain over Stage 1 is small. The forward divergence spreads the student over all the tokens the teacher allows, so the student names an entity wherever the amplified teacher gives it some probability. It reaches the highest Ent-R (0.131) and K-strict (0.145), but one in five of its entity mentions is name from Baldurs Gate 3 (0.193, against 0.010 for the full model), and its LiveU and FinalQ fall to 4.82 and 3.31, the lowest of all variants. All three loss variants also lower FinalQ. Weaker teachers keep the quality of the commentary but add less knowledge. teacher that only knows which received entries the human names, or one that checks them on screen with frozen VLM, reaches an Ent-R of 0.093 or 0.102. Only the full recipe, the reverse divergence with amplification and the ideal answer, improves all knowledge and judge metrics over Stage 1, raising Ent-R to 0.116 and K-strict to 0.127 without leaking names from the source game. Figure 4 Stage 2 variants. Dashed line: Stage 1.

sections.title: 4.8 Qualitative examples
sections.content: Fig. 5 shows StreamDuo and Proact-VL at the same seconds of seven unseen games. In the first five examples the commentator asks and, two seconds later, names what the answer contains. In StarCraft II it names Byuns Ghost Academy, which the human caster also names, and the player GuMiho in another match. In Elden Ring and Minecraft the entry is also on screen, in the equipment menu, the chest and the skill slot of Thopss Barrier, so the research agent finds it from the frames although the commentator cannot read it. The answers are not clean. Each holds up to three entries, and the commentator mostly keeps the ones that match the frames, Bloodhounds Fang but not Bloodhounds Finesse or Slash, and the golden apple but not the enchanted one. It does not always filter well, and in StarCraft II it also repeats the Warden Support Alpha, an entry unrelated to the match. Proact-VL speaks at the same seconds but stays vague, as in Wait, this is weapon, names the wrong potion, or calls an Elden Ring enemy group the Sharran, 9 Figure 5 Examples on unseen games, with the frame at the second the research agents answer arrives. Orange entries are used by the commentator, and gray ones are not. Proact-VL is retrained on the same data and shown at the same seconds, and names from Baldurs Gate 3 are in red. faction of Baldurs Gate 3. The last three examples show what happens without question. In Tears of the Kingdom, Street Fighter 6 and Black Myth: Wukong the commentator does not ask, since its ask score stays below the threshold. StreamDuo describes the scene without name, while Proact-VL fills in names from its training game, addressing character as Karlach, saying fighter has been playing Karlach, and calling boss Tiefling. Such names are not rare. Over all test clips, names from the source game make up 9.9% of the entity mentions of Proact-VL, 200 of its 2,011, and 1.0% of ours, 34 of 3,363, although StreamDuo names almost twice as many entities. Without an answer, the commentator leaves name out instead of borrowing one from the game it was trained on.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied cross-game streaming commentary, in which model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and found that current streaming commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge. To address this, StreamDuo pairs trainable commentator with frozen research agent that it asks with its frames and that answers from the games wiki while the stream continues. Information-gain labels teach the commentator when an answer is worth asking for, and on-policy self-distillation from privileged copy of itself teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldurs Gate 3 alone, StreamDuo names more of what is on screen in ten unseen games, rarely falls back on names from its training game, and keeps the timing and quality of the strongest streaming commentators, without any training on the ten games it is tested on.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: A Source-game leakage commentator trained on one game can fill an entity it does not know with name it memorized from that game. We call this source-game leakage and measure it as the share of Baldurs Gate 3 names among all entity names model says in the unseen games, counting only names that exist neither in the test game nor in its wiki. Tab. 5 reports it for all models trained on Baldurs Gate 3, on all 2,470 clips and without word cap. The two models that speak the most entity names before StreamDuo leak the most. 17.3% of the names said by StreamingVLM and 9.9% of those said by Proact-VL come from Baldurs Gate 3, such as Karlach in Street Fighter 6 or Laezel in League of Legends. Leakage is worst in esports, where the commentary is full of player and champion names the model has never seen. In League of Legends, 54.6% of the names said by Proact-VL come from Baldurs Gate 3, against 7.8% for StreamDuo. The agent dossier lowers the overall share only little, to 14.7% and 6.3%, since it lists the entities of the game but cannot tell which one is on screen. The other baselines leak less because they name few entities at all, with fewer than 900 test-game 14 Table 5 Source-game leakage on all 2,470 test clips, without word cap. Mentions: names of the test game. Leaked: Baldurs Gate 3 names that exist neither in the test game nor in its wiki. Leakage: share of leaked names among all names said. Method Mentions Leaked Leakage VideoLLM-online [6] + agent dossier LiveCC-7B-Instruct [7] + agent dossier MMDuet [42] + agent dossier StreamingVLM [46] + agent dossier MMDuet2 [43] + agent dossier Proact-VL [47] + agent dossier StreamDuo (ours) 372 676 217 867 298 99 1,271 1,188 147 135 1,811 2,533 3,329 14 1 2 4 0 1 265 205 4 2 200 170 3.6% 0.1% 0.9% 0.5% 0.0% 1.0% 17.3% 14.7% 2.6% 1.5% 9.9% 6.3% 1.0% names over all 2,470 clips. low share then says little about their knowledge. StreamDuo names the most entities of the test games, 3,329, and keeps leakage at 1.0%. Each part of StreamDuo contributes to this. Run with the same inference settings as StreamDuo, the recipe of Proact-VL leaks 5.8% of its names. Random renaming with the dossier in context (Stage 0) lowers this to 2.1%, since name from the source game is no longer reliable evidence during training. Learning when to ask (Stage 1) lowers it further to 0.8%. With asking disabled at test time, the full model leaks 2.9%, three times as much as with asking. When the commentator does not know an entity, it asks the research agent instead of reaching for name from the source game. The loss of Stage 2 matters as well. With the forward instead of the reverse divergence, leakage rises to 19.3%, the highest of all models, because the student learns to name an entity wherever the teacher gives it some probability (Sec. 4.6). Max 0.628 0.011 0.188 0.713 0.332 live commentator has to keep up with the stream, and an answer is only useful if it arrives while the entity is still on screen. Tab. 6 measures both agents on one H100 GPU with one request at time, as in live stream, using the same models, prompts and settings as in all other experiments. The research agent answers in 0.41 on average and in at most 0.71 over 200 test moments, so every answer is ready before the 2 at which StreamDuo places it in the history. The delay of 2 therefore leaves margin of more than second, and slower or larger agent would still fit. Most of this time goes to proposing search keys from the frames (0.32 s). Picking up to three entries from the retrieved candidates takes 0.08 s, and the BM25 search over the wiki takes about 2 ms. Building the search index is done once before the stream and takes 1.5 s. The commentator needs 0.26 of compute for each second of video, about four times faster than real time, and at most 0.33 on the slowest of 20 test clips. This includes decoding the frames, the speak and ask heads and the generation of each line. All 20 clips are mostly spoken, so the measurement covers the most expensive case. The research agent runs in parallel and is called only when the commentator asks. In one test run, the commentator asked 264 times over the 26 hours of test video, about once every six minutes, and in 243 of the 2,470 clips. The research agent is therefore idle most of the time, and its cost adds little to that of the commentator. StreamDuo can commentate live stream on two GPUs, one for each agent.

sections.title: B More qualitative examples
sections.content: Fig. 6 and Fig. 7 show 32 more examples from all ten unseen games, none of them in Fig. 5. Each card shows the frame at the given time, the entries that the research agent returns, StreamDuos commentary and that of Proact-VL, retrained on the same data, at the same seconds. All text is the models own output; . . . marks cut. In 21 examples the commentator asks and names what the answer contains within few seconds. The entries cover the main kinds of game knowledge: players and units in StarCraft II (ByuN, Mothership, Liberator), items and equipment in Elden Ring and Minecraft (Radahns Greaves, Goldmasks Set, the enchantments of diamond chestplate), places in Tears of the Kingdom (Rito Village, Tabantha Tundra) and skills in Cyberpunk 2077 (Short Circuit, Breach Protocol). The commentator does not repeat every entry. It keeps the Dusk Claymore but not the Dusk Bow, and the Zonaite Sword but not the Strong Zonaite Sword. It sometimes reads the wiki entry instead of commenting on the game, as in Rosalind Myers is the third and current president. . . or Brightcap, mushroom that grows in. . . . In the other 11 examples no question is asked. StreamDuo then describes the action or reads name off the screen, such as Elphael, Brace of the Haligtree in Elden Ring. At these seconds Proact-VL names characters, creatures and places from Baldurs Gate 3: Laezel and the Mind Flayers in League of Legends, Karlach in Counter-Strike 2, Street Fighter 6, Yu-Gi-Oh! and Tears of the Kingdom, and the Underdark in Black Myth: Wukong. In the examples where StreamDuo asks, Proact-VL at the same seconds names none of the entries and stays vague, as in Okay, Ill try this one. or How do we get back down?. 16 Figure 6 More examples from the ten unseen games, with StreamDuo and Proact-VL at the same seconds (1/2). Chips: the entries in the research agents answer, in orange those the commentator names. Red: names from Baldurs Gate 3. Figure 7 More examples from the ten unseen games (2/2).
